Chapter 9: Navigating Media, Technology, and the Wider World
These days, everywhere you look—on social media, in ads, even in the games kids play—there’s this steady stream of messages about gender, identity, and what it means to be “worthy.”
Now, some of this can be inspiring or help kids feel connected, but let’s be honest: a lot of it just repeats old stereotypes or sets up expectations no one can actually meet. So, how do we help kids find their way through all that noise while staying true to feminist values?
The first step is building something called media literacy. That’s just a fancy way of saying: teaching kids how to look at what they see online or on TV, and really think about it, instead of just soaking it all in.
One of the best ways to do this? Watch a show together, scroll through some social media posts, or read an article side by side. Then, just talk about it. Ask questions like, “What do you think this ad wants us to believe?” or “How does this character make you feel?”
It’s all about getting kids to pause and reflect, instead of just accepting what’s on the screen.
There are a few other practical things you can try, too. Set some boundaries around screen time, and explain why those limits matter—not just because “I said so,” but because it helps everyone stay balanced.
Encourage your child to look for stories and images that show lots of different kinds of people—different genders, backgrounds, and experiences. And talk openly about what to do if they run into bullying or harassment online, so they know how to protect themselves and others.
Here’s something really important: kids learn more from what you do than what you say. So, if you make a point to put your own devices away during dinner, or you set aside time for family without screens, you’re showing them that technology is useful, but it doesn’t run the show.
Of course, the challenges don’t stop at the screen. Kids are going to face sexism, discrimination, and exclusion in the wider world, too. That’s why it helps to practice—maybe by role-playing what to do if someone tells a sexist joke, or brainstorming ways to stand up for a friend who’s being treated unfairly.
When you give kids the words and the confidence to speak up, you’re helping them become strong advocates—not just for themselves, but for others, too.
